'''Kaurna''' ({{IPAc-en|ˈ|ɡ|ɑːr|n|ə}} or {{IPAc-en|ˈ|ɡ|aʊ|n|ə}}) is a [[Pama–Nyungan languages|Pama-Nyungan language]] historically spoken by the [[Kaurna]] peoples of the [[Adelaide Plains]] of [[South Australia]]. The Kaurna peoples are made up of various tribal clan groups, each with their own ''parnkarra'' district of land and local dialect. These dialects were historically spoken in the area bounded by [[Crystal Brook, South Australia|Crystal Brook]] and [[Clare, South Australia|Clare]] in the north, [[Cape Jervis (headland)|Cape Jervis]] in the south, and just over the [[Mount Lofty Ranges]]. Kaurna ceased to be spoken on an everyday basis in the 19th century and the last known native speaker, [[Ivaritji]], died in 1929. [[Language revival]] efforts began in the 1980s, with the language now frequently used for ceremonial purposes, such as [[dual naming]] and [[welcome to country]] ceremonies.

==Classification==
[[Robert M. W. Dixon]] (2002) classified Kaurna as a [[dialect]] of the Kadli language, along with [[Ngadjuri language|Ngadjuri]], [[Narungga language|Narungga]], and [[Nukunu language|Nukunu]], and "Nantuwara",<ref>{{cite book|first=R. M. W. |last=Dixon | author-link=Robert M. W. Dixon |title=Australian Languages: Their Nature and Development |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]] |year=2002 |url=http://www.cambridge.org/catalogue/catalogue.asp?isbn=0521473780|isbn=0-521-47378-0 }}</ref> with ''kadli'' meaning "dog" in these varieties. However this name has not gained wide acceptance and is not recorded as a language in the [[Australian Institute of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Studies#AUSTLANG|AIATSIS AUSTLANG]] database.<ref>{{AIATSIS|L61|Kadli}}</ref>

[[Luise Hercus]] and J. Simpson (2002, 2006) classify Kaurna as within the subgroup of [[Thura-Yura languages]].<ref name=AIATSIS/><ref>{{AIATSIS|L63|Thura / Yura}}</ref>

==Name==
The name "Kaurna" was not widely used until popularised by South Australian Museum [[Ethnographer]] [[Norman Tindale|Norman B. Tindale]] in the 1920s.<ref name=Amerybook>{{cite book |title=Warrabarna Kaurna! - reclaiming an Australian Language |last=Amery |first=Rob |year= 2000 |pages = 1, 3, 17 |publisher=Swets & Zeitlinger |location= The Netherlands |isbn=90-265-1633-9 }}</ref> The term "Kaurna" was first recorded by Missionary Surgeon [[William Wyatt (settler)|William Wyatt]] (1879: 24) for "Encounter Bay Bob's Tribe". At the same time he recorded "Meeyurna" for "[[Onkaparinga Jack]]'s Tribe".{{citation needed|date=July 2021}}

Kaurna most likely derives from ''kornar'', the word for "people" in the neighbouring [[Ngarrindjeri language|Ramindjeri/Ngarrindjeri language]]. [[Mullawirraburka]] (Onkaparinga Jack, also known to the colonists as "King John"), was one of [[Lutheran]] missionaries [[Christian Teichelmann]] and [[Clamor Schürmann]]'s main sources. [[Encounter Bay Bob]], as his name suggests, came from [[Encounter Bay]] (Victor Harbor) and was most likely a fully initiated elder Ramindjeri man. Thus "Meyunna" is probably the group's [[endonym]], however, they are now universally known as the Kaurna people.

===Name variants===

[[Library of Congress Subject Headings]] gives the following variant names (all followed by "language"): Adelaide; Coorna; Gauna; Gaurna; Gawurna; Kaura; Kawurna.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://lccn.loc.gov/sh85071766|access-date=27 April 2019|title=Kaurna language|website=Library of Congress Authorities}}</ref>

The [[Endangered Languages Project]] names the following alternatives: Kaura, Coorna, Koornawarra, Nganawara, Kurumidlanta, Milipitingara, Widninga, Winnaynie, Meyu, Winaini, Winnay-nie, Wakanuwan, Adelaide tribe, Warra, Warrah, Karnuwarra, Jaitjawar:a, Padnaindi, Padnayndie, Medaindi, Medain-die, Merildekald, Merelde, Gaurna, Nantuwara, Nantuwaru, Meljurna, Midlanta.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.endangeredlanguages.com/lang/5871|title= Kaurna [aka Kaura, Coorna, Koornawarra] |website=Endangered Languages Project|access-date=27 April 2019}}</ref>

== History ==

=== Early records of the language ===
{{see also|Piltawodli}}
French explorer [[Joseph Paul Gaimard]] recorded the first wordlist of the language, containing 168 words, after calling in at the [[Gulf St Vincent]] en route to [[Western Australia]] in 1826, before the [[colony of South Australia]] had been established. His sources were listed as Harry and Sally.<ref name=adelaidia>{{cite web | last=Amery | first=Rob | title=Kaurna language (Kaurna warra) | website=Adelaidia | date=9 December 2013 | url=https://adelaidia.history.sa.gov.au/subjects/kaurna-language-kaurna-warra | access-date=13 July 2021}}</ref>

Schürmann and Teichelmann, who ran a school at [[Piltawodli]], gained most of their knowledge of the language from three respected [[Aboriginal elder|elders]]: [[Mullawirraburka]] ("King John" / "Onkaparinga Jack"), [[Kadlitpinna]] ("Captain Jack") and [[Ityamai-itpina|Ityamaiitpinna]] ("[King Rodney"). The two missionaries recorded around about 3000 words, a sketch [[linguistic description|grammar]], hundreds of phrases and sentences along with English translations, traditional [[songline]]s, and textual illustrations of differences among dialects. They also created Kaurna translations of six German [[hymn]]s as well as the [[Ten Commandments]].<ref name=adelaidia/>

Other Europeans such as [[William Wyatt (settler)|William Wyatt]], [[William Williams (brewer)|William Williams]],<ref>{{cite web|format=photo and text|website=State Library of South Australia|url=https://collections.slsa.sa.gov.au/resource/B+5839|title=William Williams [B 5839]: Photograph|access-date=9 December 2019}} ).</ref><ref name=amery2016>{{cite book | last=Amery | first=Rob | title=Warraparna Kaurna!: Reclaiming an Australian language | publisher=[[University of Adelaide Press]] | series=JSTOR Open Access monographs | year=2016 | isbn=978-1-925261-25-7 | chapter-url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.20851/j.ctt1sq5wgq.13|url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.20851/j.ctt1sq5wgq.13|chapter=4. A Sociolinguistic History of Kaurna  | access-date=11 January 2021 | pages=57–68| jstor=10.20851/j.ctt1sq5wgq.13 }} (Also [https://www.adelaide.edu.au/press/system/files/2019-04/uap-kaurna-ebook.pdf here])</ref> [[William Cawthorne]] and [[Matthew Moorhouse]] were interested in the people and learnt some of the language; several wrote about the "Adelaide Tribe" in their memoirs.<ref name=griffith>{{cite web|publisher=[[Griffith University]]|website=German missionaries in Australia|url=http://missionaries.griffith.edu.au/mission/piltawodli-native-location-1838-1845|title=Piltawodli Native Location (1838-1845)|first=Rob|last=Amery|access-date=8 December 2019|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name=amery2016/> Williams created a list of 377 Kaurna words, published in the ''[[Southern Australian]]'' on 15 May 1839 and republished in ''[[The South Australian Colonist]]''<ref name=griffith/> on 14 July 1840.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Williams|first=William|date=14 July 1840|title=The language of the natives of South Australia|journal=[[South Australian Colonist]]|volume=1|issue=19|pages=295–296|url=http://www.nla.gov.au/ferguson/1461426X/18400714/00010019/7-9.pdf|via=[[Australian Cooperative Digitisation Project]]. Australian Periodical Publications 1840–1845|access-date=11 January 2021|archive-date=13 January 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210113103225/http://www.nla.gov.au/ferguson/1461426X/18400714/00010019/7-9.pdf|url-status=dead}} (Access page [http://www.nla.gov.au/ferg/issn/1461426X.html here] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210118021821/http://www.nla.gov.au/ferg/issn/1461426X.html |date=18 January 2021 }}.</ref><ref name=karrwadlungga>{{cite journal | last=Schultz | first=Chester|publisher=[[University of Adelaide]] | title=Karrawadlungga | website=Adelaide Research & Scholarship | date=13 August 2020 | hdl=2440/113971| url=http://hdl.handle.net/2440/113971 | access-date=12 January 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Karrawadlungga| date=13 August 2020|series=Place Name Summary (PNS) 9/04|last=Schultz | first=Chester|quote=...with some more thoughts on the ‘Wirra tribe’. and PART 3 of the 1839 Police expedition|url=https://www.adelaide.edu.au/kwp/placenames/research-publ/9-04Karrawadlungg.pdf}}</ref>  His work entitled ''A vocabulary of the language of the Aborigines of the Adelaide district, and other friendly tribes, of the Province of South Australia'' was self-published in 1839, to be sold in London as well as Adelaide.<ref>{{Citation | author1=Williams, William | title=A vocabulary of the language of the Aborigines of the Adelaide district, and other friendly tribes, of the Province of South Australia | publication-date=1839 | publisher=Published for the author by A. In the 19th century, there was also a Kaurna-based [[pidgin]] used as a contact language.{{citation needed|date=January 2021}}

The former range of the language was mapped by [[Norman Tindale]] and later [[Robert Amery]], and is managed by the Kaurna people.{{citation needed|date=July 2021}}

=== Language revival ===
Kaurna had not been spoken as a native language since the Kaurna people had been pushed out of their traditional lands since the [[colonisation of South Australia]] in the 19th century, with the population in decline due to various factors.<ref name=dict/> [[Ivaritji]] ({{circa}}1849–1929) was the last known speaker, but it was probably last only widely spoken in the early 1860s.<ref name=adelaidia/>

In the 1980s, Kaurna people who had moved back into the [[Adelaide Plains]] area  began to learn and use their language again.<ref name=dict>{{cite web | title=The Kaurna Language Dictionary (forthcoming)|website= Kaurna Warra Pintyanthi | publisher=The University of Adelaide | date=11 July 2021 | url=https://www.adelaide.edu.au/kwp/resources/kaurnadictionary/ | access-date=13 July 2021}}</ref> [[Robert Amery]], head of Linguistics at the [[University of Adelaide]], who has devoted much of his life and career to Indigenous languages, in particular Kaurna: "After more than 25 years of painstaking effort, there are now several Kaurna people who can conduct a conversation in Kaurna without resorting to English too quickly, and we are seeing the first semi-native speakers of Kaurna emerging".<ref name=Ameryprof/> Kaurna is now frequently used to give [[Welcomes to Country]].<ref name=dict/><ref name=adelaidia/>

Sustained efforts to revive the language in from 1989 included the writing of several Kaurna songs originally written in the [[Ngarrindjeri language|Ngarrindjeri]], [[Narangga language|Narungga]] and Kaurna languages. A second songbook, ''Kaurna Paltinna'', was published in 1999. Following one-off workshops in 1990 and 1991,{{citation needed|date=July 2019}} a Kaurna language program was introduced into [[Kaurna Plains School]] in 1992. Elizabeth City High School and Elizabeth West Adult Campus introduced the teaching of the language in 1994, and other schools have followed suit. [[TAFE]] courses to train Kaurna language teachers were developed by Mary-Anne Gale. Kaurna linguistics courses have been taught at the [[University of Adelaide]] since 1997.<ref name=adelaidia/><ref name=Ameryprof>{{cite web|website=University of Adelaide|title=Dr Robert Amery|url=https://researchers.adelaide.edu.au/profile/robert.amery|access-date=4 July 2019}}</ref> and both Kaurna and non-Kaurna have been studying and speaking the language.<ref name=dict/>

The records, including an extensive vocabulary and grammar, compiled by Teichelmann and Schürmann in the 1840s have proven valuable in projects to reconstruct the language.<ref>{{cite book|title=Colonialism and its Aftermath: A history of Aboriginal South Australia|chapter-url=https://www.wakefieldpress.com.au/product.php?productid=1385|publisher=[[Wakefield Press (Australia)|Wakefield Press]]|isbn=9781743054994|date=2017|editor1-first=Peggy|editor1-last=Brock|editor2-first=Tom|editor2-last=Gara|chapter=4. Early encounters on the Adelaide Plains and Encounter Bay|first1=Christine|last1=Lockwood|pages=65–81|archive-date=21 October 2022|access-date=4 July 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221021032937/https://www.wakefieldpress.com.au/product.php?productid=1385|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name=adelaidia/><ref>{{cite book|first=C. G. |last=Teichelmann |author2=C. W. Schürmann |title=Outlines of a grammar, vocabulary and phraseology of the Aboriginal language of South Australia spoken by the natives in and for some distance around Adelaide|publisher=Lutheran Missionary Society, Adelaide|year=1840 |url=https://digital.library.adelaide.edu.au/dspace/handle/2440/116578 }}</ref>

The ''Kaurna Learners' Guide'' (''Kulurdu Marni Ngathaitya'') was published in 2013, and Kaurna radio shows have been broadcast since 2012. The Kaurna Dictionary Project at the [[University of Adelaide]], funded by a federal government grant, is under way to revise the spellings. Amery has been overseeing much of the work. It is intended that the final version will be released in print and in electronic form, including a [[phone app]].<ref name=KWPlang>{{cite web|url=https://www.adelaide.edu.au/kwp/projects/|website=Kaurna WarraPintyanthi|title=Language projects|access-date=4 July 2019}}</ref> In 2021, a printed Kaurna dictionary was published, as well as a Ngarrindjeri one. Amery and his wife, Ngarrindjeri linguist Mary-Anne Gale, have helped to drive the project.<ref name="Marchant 2021"/>

There has been a growing number of Kaurna speakers in the 21st century.<ref name="bbc_revival_article">{{cite web |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/world-asia-20066624 |title=Lost indigenous language revived in Australia |author=Phil Mercer |date=22 January 2013 |work=BBC |access-date=22 January 2013}}</ref><ref name=adelaidia/>

The first students of courses specially tailored to the teaching of [[Aboriginal Australian languages|Aboriginal language]], run by [[Tauondi Aboriginal College]] in [[Port Adelaide]], enabling those who have learnt the language to pass on their skills to communities, graduated in July 2021.<ref name="Marchant 2021">{{cite web | last=Marchant | first=Gabriella | website=ABC News | title=Aboriginal languages making comeback through new training program and dictionaries | date=12 July 2021 | url=https://www.abc.net.au/news/2021-07-11/aboriginal-languages-boosted-by-new-dictionaries-and-education/100275646 | access-date=13 July 2021}}</ref> With the teachers and students often in the older age group, by July 2022 two of the first graduates had died. There is a need for more funding and more teachers.<ref>{{cite web | title=Real talk at Tauondi Aboriginal Community College | website=[[CityMag]] |first =Angela |last =Skujins| date=7 July 2022 | url=https://citymag.indaily.com.au/happening/knowledge/real-talk-at-tauondi-aboriginal-community-college/ | access-date=16 July 2022}}</ref>

===Kaurna Warra Pintyanthi===
[[Kaurna Warra Pintyanthi]] (meaning "creating Kaurna language") is a group developing and promoting the recovery of the Kaurna language. It was established in 2002 by two Kaurna [[Aboriginal elder|elders]], [[Lewis Yerloburka O'Brien]] and [[Alitya Rigney|Alitya Wallara Rigney]], and linguist [[Robert Amery]]. The group now includes other Kaurna people, teachers, linguists and language enthusiasts. It was created from a series of workshops funded by a [[University of Adelaide]] grant in 2000, and is hosted by the department of linguistics at the University of Adelaide.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://adelaide.edu.au/kwp/ |title=Kaurna Warra Pintyanthi |access-date=31 August 2015 |archive-date=27 September 2006 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060927080553/http://adelaide.edu.au/kwp/ |url-status=dead }}</ref> KWP-run language classes through both the [[Kaurna Plains School]] and the university.

KWP has created a uniform dialect of the language, making new words such as ''mukarntu'' (''mukamuka'' brain + ''karntu'' lightning), meaning "computer", and other words for things such as modern appliances, transportation, cuisine, and other common features of life that have changed for the Kaurna people while the language was dormant.<ref name="kwp_formingwords">{{cite book|first1=Rob |last1=Amery |first2=Jane |last2=Simpson |date=2013 |title=Kulurdu Marni Ngathaitya |publisher=Kaurna Warrarna Pintyanthi, Wakefield Press |page=171}}</ref> The Kaurna Warra Karrpanthi Aboriginal Corporation (KWK) was registered in 2013 to support the reclamation and promotion of the language of the Kaurna nation, including training and teaching.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.adelaide.edu.au/kwp/kwk/ |title=Kaurna Warra Karrpanthi Aboriginal Corporation (KWK) |publisher=Kaurna Warra Pintyanthi |date=15 February 2015 |access-date=31 August 2015}}</ref>

===Dictionary===

In 2022 a [[dictionary]] written by Rob Amery and co-authors Susie Greenwood and Jasmin Morley was published. It includes not only the words included on the handwritten lists made by Teichelmann and Schürmann 160 years earlier, but also 4,000 new words that were created in consultation with local [[Aboriginal elder|elders]] and Kaurna speakers. The cover was designed by Kaurna artist Katrina Karlapina Power.<ref>{{cite web | last=Randall | first=Angus | title=How Adelaide's 'extinct' Indigenous language Kaurna was brought back to life  | website=ABC News |publisher= [[Australian Broadcasting Corporation]] | date=4 August 2022 | url=https://www.abc.net.au/news/2022-08-04/indigenous-language-kaurna-brought-back-to-life-in-dictionary/101301262 | access-date=5 August 2022}}</ref> Entitled ''Kaurna Warrapiipa, Kaurna Dictionary'', the dictionary contains translations both ways (Kaurna and [[English language|English]]). and is published by [[Wakefield Press (Australia)|Wakefield Press]].<ref>{{cite book | title=Kaurna Warrapiipa, Kaurna Dictionary|isbn= 9781743059210| date=2022 | url=https://www.wakefieldpress.com.au/product.php?productid=1783 | access-date=5 August 2022|last1= Amery|first1= Rob|last2= Greenwood |first2= Susie|last3= Morley|first3= Jasmin|publisher= Kaurna Warra Pintyanthi}}</ref>

==Phonology==
===Vowels===
Kaurna has three different vowels with contrastive long and short lengths (a, i, u, a:, i:, u:), and three diphthongs (ai, au, ui).<ref name="kwp_vowels">{{cite book|title=Kulurdu Marni Ngathaitya |page=31}}</ref> The three main vowels are represented by ⟨a⟩, ⟨i⟩ and ⟨u⟩ respectively, with long vowels indicated by doubling the vowel. Historically, Kaurna has had ⟨e⟩ and ⟨o⟩ used varyingly in older versions of its orthography, but these are not reflected in the phonology of the language.

===Consonants===
The consonant inventory of Kaurna is similar to that of other Pama-Nyungan languages (compare with [[Adnyamathanha language|Adnyamathanha]], in the same [[Thura-Yura languages|Thura-Yura]] grouping). In the orthography, dental consonants are followed by {{grapheme|h}} and palatals by {{grapheme|y}}, and retroflex consonants are preceded by {{grapheme|r}}, with the exception of {{grapheme|rd}} {{IPA|/ɾ/}}. Pre-stopped consonants are preceded by {{grapheme|d}}. Below are the consonants of Kaurna (Amery, R & Simpson, J 2013<ref>{{cite book|title=Kulurdu Marni Ngathaitya |pages=29–30}}</ref>).

===Phonotactics===
* All words must begin with a [[Peripheral consonant|peripheral]] or [[laminal]] consonant (see [[#Consonants|Consonants]] above), excluding the pre-stopped nasals.
* All words must end with a vowel.
* In addition to the pre-stopped consonants, consonant clusters of a nasal followed by a stop are allowed.<ref>{{cite book|title=Kulurdu Marni Ngathaitya |pages=31–32}}</ref>

===Prosody===
Kaurna places primary stress on the first syllable.<ref name="kwp_vowels" />

==Grammar==
Kaurna has relatively [[free word order]].<ref>{{cite book|title=Kulurdu Marni Ngathaitya |pages=114–115}}</ref>

====Number====
Kaurna has 3 numbers: [[Singular (grammatical number)|singular]], [[Dual (grammatical number)|dual]] (-rla, -dla) and [[plural]] (-rna).<ref name="noun_suffixes" />

== Kaurna names ==

===Renaming and dual naming===

Efforts to reintroduce Kaurna names, beginning in 1980 with the naming of [[Warriappendi School]],<ref>{{cite web |title=Who are we? |url=http://www.warriappendi.sa.edu.au/index.htm |access-date=27 April 2019 |website=Warriapendi School |archive-date=5 March 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190305011840/http://warriappendi.sa.edu.au/index.htm |url-status=dead }}</ref> in 1980 by Auntie [[Leila Rankine]], have been made within the public domain.<ref name="adelaidia" />

Since the [[Adelaide City Council]] drew up a Reconciliation Vision Statement in 1997, they committed to a [[dual naming]] project, working with Kaurna Warra Pintyanthi, to cover the [[Adelaide city centre|city centre]] and [[North Adelaide]], including the five [[public square]]s and [[Adelaide park lands]]. [[Victoria Square, Adelaide|Victoria Square]], in the centre of Adelaide city, is now also known as ''Tarntanyangga'',<ref>{{cite web |title=Victoria Square/Tarntanyangga |url=https://adelaideparklands.com.au/parks-and-squares/victoria-square-tarntanyangga |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190427083524/https://adelaideparklands.com.au/parks-and-squares/victoria-square-tarntanyangga |archive-date=27 April 2019 |access-date=27 April 2019 |website=City of Adelaide}}</ref> all 29 Parks around the city have been assigned a Kaurna name, and the [[River Torrens]] is now also named ''Karrawirra Parri''.<ref>{{cite web |title=Adelaide City Council Placenaming Initiatives |url=https://www.adelaide.edu.au/kwp/placenames/council/ |access-date=27 April 2019 |website=Kaurna Warra Pintyanthi}}</ref> The renaming of 39 sites was finalised and endorsed by the council in 2012.<ref>{{cite web |title=Kaurna place naming: Recognising Kaurna heritage through physical features of the city |url=https://www.cityofadelaide.com.au/community/reconciliation/kaurna-place-naming/ |access-date=29 November 2019 |website=City of Adelaide}}</ref> Others include Piltawodli (now [[Pirltawardli]]), "[[brushtail possum]] home";  Warriparringga ([[Warriparinga]]) "windy river place".{{citation needed|date=July 2021}} The full list of square and park names, along with meanings and pronunciations, is available on the Council website.<ref name="SignSites">{{cite web |title=Kaurna Place Naming |url=https://www.cityofadelaide.com.au/your-community/culture-history/kaurna/place-naming/sign-sites |access-date=14 December 2019 |website=City of Adelaide}}</ref>

Between 1980 and 2012, around 1000 entities were assigned Kaurna names, including people, pets, organisations, buildings, parks, walking trails, an [[allele]] (a hereditary gene or chromosome), brand names, and the Kari Munaintya tram and Tindo solar bus.<ref name="adelaidia" />

Some place names are known from historical sources, but not officially used as yet, such as Patpangga ([[Rapid Bay, South Australia|Rapid Bay]]) "in the south"; Pattawilyangga (Patawalonga, [[Glenelg, South Australia|Glenelg]]) "swamp gum foliage"; and Yertabulti ([[Port Adelaide]]).<ref>Amery, Rob & Williams, Georgina Yambo (2002). "Reclaiming Through Renaming: The Reinstatement of Kaurna Toponyms in Adelaide and the Adelaide Plains." In [[Luise Hercus]], Flavia Hodges & Jane Simpson (eds) ''The Land is a Map: Placenames of Indigenous Origin in Australia'', 255–276.</ref>

Public artworks, beginning in 1995 with the Yerrakartarta installation outside the Intercontinental Hotel on [[North Terrace, Adelaide]], have also incorporated words, phrases and text drawn from the Kaurna language, and the universities and other organisations have also taken on Kaurna names.<ref>{{cite web |title=Kaurna Language in Public Art and Commemorative Plaques within the city precincts |url=https://www.adelaide.edu.au/kwp/public/art/ |access-date=27 April 2019 |website=Kaurna Warra Pintyanthi}}</ref> The [[Tandanya National Aboriginal Cultural Institute]] uses the original name for Adelaide.<ref>{{cite web |title=Organisations with Kaurna Names within the Adelaide City Precincts |url=https://www.adelaide.edu.au/kwp/public/organisations/ |access-date=27 April 2019 |website=Kaurna Warra Pintyanthi |publisher=University of Adelaide}}</ref>

The annual [[Tarnanthi]] Festival of Contemporary Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Art takes its name from the Kaurna word meaning "to rise, come forth, spring up or appear".<ref name="SMH2017">{{cite news |last=Mcdonald |first=John |date=31 October 2017 |title=Review: Tarnanthi, Festival of Contemporary Aboriginal and Torres Strait Island Art |url=https://www.smh.com.au/entertainment/art-and-design/review-tarnanthi-festival-of-contemporary-aboriginal-and-torres-strait-island-art-20171031-gzbh9n.html |access-date=26 April 2019 |publisher=Sydney Morning Herald}}</ref>

===Other Kaurna-derived names===
Many prominent South Australian place names are drawn from the Kaurna language:
* Kauandilla ([[Cowandilla]]) from ''kauanda'' meaning "north" plus locative suffix ''-illa'';<ref name="LandIsAMapCh10">{{Citation |last1=Amery |first1=Rob |title=The Land is a Map: Placenames of Indigenous Origin in Australia |date=March 2009 |pages=202–203 |editor1-last=Hercus |editor1-first=Luise |url=http://press.anu.edu.au?p=29191 |chapter=Chapter 10. Pinning down Kaurna names: Linguistic issues arising in the development of the Kaurna Placenames Database |chapter-url=http://press-files.anu.edu.au/downloads/press/p286811/pdf/ch101.pdf |publisher=ANU Press |isbn=9781921536571 |last2=Buckskin |first2=Vincent (Jack) Kanya |editor2-last=Hodges |editor2-first=Flavia |editor3-last=Simpson |editor3-first=Jane}}</ref>
* Kanggarilla ([[Kangarilla]]) from ''kanggari'' meaning "shepherding" plus locative suffix ''-illa'';<ref name="LandIsAMapCh10" />
* [[Kondoparinga, South Australia|Kondoparinga]] possibly from ''kundo'' meaning "chest" plus ''parri'' meaning "river" plus locative suffix ''-ngga'';<ref name="LandIsAMapCh10" />
* Maitpangga ([[Myponga, South Australia|Myponga]]);
* Ngaltingga ([[Aldinga, South Australia|Aldinga]]) from ''ngalti'' (meaning unknown) plus locative suffix ''-ngga'';<ref name="LandIsAMapCh10" />
* Ngangkiparringga ([[Onkaparinga River|Onkaparinga]]) from ''nganki'' meaning "woman" plus ''parri'' meaning "river" plus locative suffix ''-ngga'';<ref name="LandIsAMapCh10" />
* Nurlongga ([[Noarlunga (disambiguation)|Noarlunga]]) ''nurlo'' meaning "corner/curavature" plus locative suffix ''-ngga'', probably in reference to Horseshoe Bend on the [[Onkaparinga River]];
* [[Patawalonga River|Patawalonga]] from ''patta'', a species of gum tree (possibly the [[Eucalyptus ovata|swamp gum]]), plus ''wilya'' meaning "foliage" plus locative suffix ''-ngga'';<ref name="LandIsAMapCh10" />
* Waitpingga ([[Waitpinga, South Australia|Waitpinga]]) meaning "wind place"
* Willangga ([[Willunga, South Australia|Willunga]])
* Wilyaru ([[Willyaroo, South Australia|Willyaroo]]) meaning a fully initiated adult man.<ref name="LandIsAMapCh10" />
* [[Yatala (disambiguation)|Yatala]]<!--intentional link to DAB page--> most likely from ''yartala'' meaning "water running by the side of a river; inundation; cascade".<ref name="LandIsAMapCh10" />
* Yernkalyilla ([[Yankalilla, South Australia|Yankalilla]]) 'place of the fallen bits'
* Yurridla ([[Uraidla]]) meaning "two ears", derived from a [[Dreamtime (mythology)|dreaming]] story in which the [[Mount Lofty Ranges]] are the body of a giant.<ref name="LandIsAMapCh10" />

English-Kaurna [[Hybrid word|hybridised]] placenames include:
* [[Glenunga, South Australia|Glenunga]] from [[Scots language]] ''glen'' and Kaurna locative suffix ''-ngga''.<ref name="LandIsAMapCh1">{{Citation |last1=Amery |first1=Rob |title=The Land is a Map: Placenames of Indigenous Origin in Australia |date=March 2009 |pages=165–180 |editor1-last=Hercus |editor1-first=Luise |url=http://press.anu.edu.au?p=29191 |chapter= 1. Indigenous Placenames: An Introduction |chapter-url=http://press-files.anu.edu.au/downloads/press/p29191/pdf/ch0125.pdf |publisher=ANU Press |isbn=9781921536571 |editor2-last=Hodges |editor2-first=Flavia |editor3-last=Simpson |editor3-first=Jane}}</ref>
* [[Paracombe, South Australia|Paracombe]] from ''para'' meaning "river/stream" and Celtic language ''combe'' (similar to Welsh 'cwm') meaning "narrow way". Similar to South Australia's 'Picadilly', there exists a direct analogue in England, [[Parracombe]] in Devon, which likely contributed to the adoption of the name.<ref>{{Citation |last=Manning |first=George |title=Place Names of South Australia: Paracombe |date=1990 |work=Manning Index of South Australian History |url=http://www.slsa.sa.gov.au/manning/pn/p/p1.htm#paracombeE |access-date=31 May 2017 |publisher=State Library of South Australia}}</ref>

Possible Kaurna placenames include:
* [[Piccadilly, South Australia|Piccadilly]]. Although usually assumed to be named after [[Piccadilly, London]], it is likely to be an [[anglicisation]] of the Kaurna ''pikodla'' meaning "two eyebrows", being a part of the same dreaming story that gave rise to "Uraidla".<ref name="LandIsAMapCh10" />
* [[Yankalilla, South Australia|Yankalilla]]. Although almost certainly an [[Aboriginal Australian languages|Indigenous word]], there are conflicting etymologies. The most likely is that it is derived from the [[Ramindjeri language|Ramindjeri]] ''yangaiake'' meaning "hill", but with the Kaurna locative suffix ''-illa'', or possibly ''yernkalyilla'' meaning "place of the fallen bits".<ref name="LandIsAMapCh10" />

Newly-created names include:
*[[Warriappendi School]]. When the school moved in 1983, the new name was chosen by [[Leila Rankine]] and her sister [[Veronica Brodie]] (who had been key players in the school's foundation), in association with [[Narungga]] man [[Peter Buckskin]], in consultation with Kaurna people. The word ''Warriappendi'' means "to seek" or "searching for", and marked the first time that Kaurna people themselves had chosen a Kaurna word for public naming purposes.<ref name=hist>{{cite web | title=The History | website=Warriappendi Secondary School | date=29 May 2025 | url=https://warriappendi.sa.edu.au/about/the-history/ | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250501121734/https://warriappendi.sa.edu.au/about/the-history/ | archive-date=1 May 2025 | url-status=live | access-date=5 November 2025}}</ref>
